title: Are Harnesses Worth the Cost?
summary: An experiment finds a behavioral harness of contracts and tests made a cheap model as reliable as a frontier model, while adding cost without benefit for the frontier model.

assertions.quote: it turned a 3-in-10 baseline into 10-for-10 reliability

verdicts.note: Supported by one small experiment on a single greenfield service with an unusually detailed brief, so the scope is unproven.

assertions.quote: The harness increased average time and cost without changing the observed acceptance result.

verdicts.note: Observed in one experiment; harder or less specified tasks may still benefit from in-loop checks.

assertions.quote: If an agent interprets requirements to write both the implementation and its tests, the same misreading or omission can appear in both.
A behavioral harness turns written requirements into environmental feedback, bringing dropped details back into focus when a sensor goes red.
Juggling library choices, boilerplate setup, dependency injection, and asynchronous wiring across a growing context may contribute to such lapses
Allowing it to change the expected results when tests fail can also obscure a defect.
Contract-driven dependency mocks made downstream interactions executable
All 10 unharnessed GPT-6 Sol applications passed every functional check on the first pass without human debugging or corrective follow-ups.
Invest in clear specifications and examples: The checks can enforce only the expectations humans encode.
